analysis.one_liner: Stops taxing Social Security benefits, paid for by payroll taxes on wages above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop taxing Social Security benefits never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, up to 85% of a retiree's Social Security check counts as taxable income once combined income passes certain thresholds, so millions of seniors pay federal income tax on benefits they earned through a lifetime of payroll taxes. This bill would remove Social Security benefits from federal taxable income entirely. To make up the money, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000 a year (wages above about $168,600 are currently exempt) and would count that newly taxed high earning toward slightly larger benefits. It also appropriates funds to keep the Social Security trust funds whole.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees who currently pay federal income tax on their Social Security checks, roughly 40-50% of beneficiaries under current rules, would keep more of their income. Middle- and upper-middle-income seniors gain the most, since the tax falls hardest on those whose benefits plus other income exceed the thresholds. High earners above $250,000 would also start earning slightly larger Social Security benefits because their newly taxed wages would count in the benefit formula.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors who pay tax on benefits

how_it_helps.text: Removes Social Security benefits from gross income for federal income tax purposes, ending the taxation of benefits beginning with the first taxable year after enactment.

Funds the change by extending the Social Security payroll tax to wages above $250,000 per year, whereas under current law wages above the contribution and benefit base (about $168,600 in 2024) are exempt; it also applies to self-employment income and includes a special rule so workers with multiple employers who cross $250,000 collectively pay the tax.

Counts newly taxed earnings above $250,000 in the benefit formula at a modest rate, so the people paying the new tax receive some additional benefit in return, and holds the Social Security and related trust funds harmless for lost revenue through appropriations.
Protects SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries from any benefit increase that would otherwise change their eligibility or benefit amounts.

analysis.who_pays: High earners — employees with wages above $250,000, self-employed people with income above that level, and high-income business owners — would pay Social Security payroll taxes on income that is currently exempt. The federal Treasury would collect those new taxes instead of income tax on benefits.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises Social Security payroll taxes on wages and self-employment income above $250,000, including a new mechanism that can hit workers whose combined wages from multiple employers cross that line, and critics of lifting the payroll cap generally argue it raises taxes on small business owners and self-employed professionals.

Eliminating the tax on benefits is expensive for the Treasury; the bill offsets it by redirecting payroll tax revenue and appropriating Treasury funds to hold the trust funds harmless, but the cost depends on the payroll-tax increase generating enough revenue to cover the income-tax cut.

The bill would also slightly increase benefits for the highest earners (2% of earnings above $250,000 counts toward the benefit formula), a provision supporters frame as reciprocity but which critics would call a giveaway to people who need it least.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a tax cut for seniors paid for by a payroll tax increase on the top slice of earners. It is structured to be solvent — trust funds are held harmless and the people paying the new tax earn somewhat larger benefits — and its protective provisions for SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP recipients show care for low-income interactions. The main honest objections are the new tax burden on high-earning workers and small business owners and the uncertainty of whether the offset covers the full cost. On its own terms it is a straightforward, progressively funded tax cut for retirees.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and a second committee, then sat in three subcommittees without a hearing or markup, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on January 25, 2024, with six original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.

It was then referred to three subcommittees — Health (January 26, 2024), and Work and Welfare and Social Security (December 17, 2024) — and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All 14 cosponsors were Democrats, and no committee action was taken on the bill in over 11 months.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirees keep nothing — seniors who pay tax on their Social Security benefits remain taxed, and high earners never face the new payroll tax above $250,000 that would have funded the repeal. The Ways and Means Committee simply never acted, so the current tax treatment of benefits continues unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled original cosponsors including Reps. Khanna, Caraveo, Davis of North Carolina, Peltola, Salinas, and Scholten.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all 14 were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair Jason Smith, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor consideration of the bill in over 11 months, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress expired.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill; jurisdiction split across two committees is a standard way referrals dilute a bill's chances.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.note: Employees and self-employed people earning above $250,000 would pay Social Security payroll taxes on income currently exempt above the cap (about $168,600), including workers whose wages from multiple employers cross the line. The exemption is a structural benefit for top earners, and the bill narrows it.

industries.industry: Small business owners and self-employed professionals
industries.note: The bill explicitly applies the new tax to self-employment income above $250,000, a group that has historically opposed lifting the payroll cap. Some would receive modestly larger Social Security benefits in return.

industries.industry: Social Security and Railroad Retirement trust funds
industries.note: The funds lose the income tax revenue that currently flows to them from taxing benefits, but the bill both redirects the new payroll tax revenue to them and appropriates Treasury funds to hold them harmless, and the extra payroll taxes add long-term revenue.
